entry.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a 26.4B-parameter looped transformer model optimized for local laptop use and agentic coding tasks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Thinking Machines has launched Inkling 2 Mini, a looped transformer model with 26.4 billion parameters designed to run efficiently on consumer laptops and desktops. The model applies its middle layers multiple times per token to enhance reasoning quality, leading open-weight models under 100 billion parameters on benchmarks like DeepSWE v1.1 and Vals Index v2.2 while maintaining faster inference speeds. Inkling 2 Mini supports longer reasoning without extensive chain-of-thought outputs, improving monitorability and performance on serial reasoning tasks. It uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with a total memory footprint of about 20GB, enabling offline use on devices such as MacBook Pros. The model excels in agentic coding and knowledge work benchmarks, leveraging search and tool use to compensate for its parameter size limitations. It is available with open weights on the Tinker platform for inference and customization.

entry.title: Researchers demonstrate a 27B parameter language model that rewrites its own weights to improve accuracy and repair itself without retraining [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A new study shows that a large language model can self-optimize by rewriting its own weights through reasoning, improving its accuracy by 6.6 points on unseen problems without gradient updates or additional training. The model tests its edits iteratively, only applying improvements that work, and can repair a damaged copy of itself to regain over 80% of original accuracy on image tasks it never encountered. This self-rewriting ability emerges only at larger scales, as smaller models fail or degrade themselves. Unlike traditional training or inference scaling, this approach embeds improvements directly into the model's weights with only forward passes, blurring the line between training and inference. The researchers suggest this could be a step toward recursive self-improvement, enabling models to continuously upgrade themselves without external intervention.

entry.title: Anthropic shares fall 12% on second trading day amid AI sector sell-off, dragging Nasdaq down 2% and wiping out 2026 gains [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Anthropic's shares dropped by as much as 12% on their second day of trading, falling close to their IPO price amid a broader sell-off in AI-related stocks that also pushed the Nasdaq down 2%. The company's volatile debut followed a 17% rise on the first day, but investor concerns about high valuations and profitability in the AI sector have dampened enthusiasm. The sell-off extended globally, with Asian markets experiencing their worst week since 2020, including significant declines in major chipmakers and tech stocks. Analysts noted that Anthropic's IPO may have drained market liquidity, forcing investors to sell other tech shares to fund their purchases. The downturn reflects growing skepticism about the sustainability of investment in AI amid rising interest rates and regulatory scrutiny, such as a subpoena issued to Nvidia over semiconductor exports to China.

entry.title: Engineer uses AI coding agents to program an FPGA for running a large language model, achieving a 33× speedup to 213 tokens per second [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: An engineer experimented with programming an FPGA to run a large language model (LLM) using AI coding agents, which autonomously wrote and optimized C++ and Verilog code. The project, conducted on AWS F2 instances with 16 GB FPGA memory, resulted in a functional LLM inference chip that improved performance from a baseline to 213 tokens per second, a 33-fold increase. The process involved running a cloud agent that iteratively refined the code over several days, producing millions of lines of code and output while costing about $10,000 in AI token usage. The engineer had limited prior experience with FPGA programming and Verilog but relied on AI models like Claude and OpenAI to handle low-level hardware coding and verification. Minimal human guidance was provided, mainly motivational prompts and occasional technical suggestions, demonstrating the potential of AI agents to tackle complex hardware programming tasks.

entry.title: RMRFBench launches to measure how often AI agents with root access destroy servers during routine file deletion tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: RMRFBench is a new benchmark tool that tests AI agents by giving them root shell access on throwaway Linux servers and instructing them to perform routine file deletion tasks. The tool evaluates how often these agents cause server damage by executing commands like 'rm -rf' incorrectly, ranking models based on server survival rather than task completion alone. Each test boots a fresh server, sets up a scenario with visible traps such as unquoted globs or empty variables, and assigns the AI a terse deletion task. After the agent runs unattended with a single bash tool, the server's state is inspected to determine if it survived without damage. The benchmark ranks models by their ability to avoid wrecking the server, emphasizing safety over mere task completion. The project publishes detailed incident reports, scoring methodology, and scenario descriptions, allowing users to understand where and why AI agents fail. It highlights the risks of granting AI root access for file operations and provides a framework to compare models' reliability and safety in such critical tasks.

entry.title: Experts warn nearly everyone in AI is vulnerable to honey-trap schemes exploiting personal relationships for corporate espionage [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Experts highlight that individuals across the AI industry, from CEOs to employees with sensitive information, are susceptible to honey-trap schemes-deceptive tactics using emotional or romantic manipulation to gain access to valuable company secrets. This risk has grown as AI companies hold critical technology and data, making personal relationships a target for espionage rather than traditional cyberattacks. The recent allegations against Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, involving a suspected honey trap linked to Chinese espionage, underscore the threat's seriousness. Attackers often pose as investors, recruiters, or consultants, using AI tools to create convincing fake identities and backstories, making detection difficult. Experts advise vigilance for unusual patterns in interactions and emphasize the need for company cultures that encourage questioning and reporting suspicious behavior to mitigate these risks.

entry.title: NEXUPIRA tests autonomous AI memory saving for small-business assistants, identifies errors and implements rules after two days of live use [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: NEXUPIRA allowed its AI assistants for small businesses to save memories autonomously without user approval, leading to errors such as misclassifying one-off requests as rules and test questions as business plans. The company observed these issues during two days of production testing and responded by adding rule-based filters and an undo feature to improve memory accuracy and user control. Initially, the AI required users to approve memory saves, but this approach failed because small-business owners rarely accessed the approval page. The new system uses text-based rules and checks to decide which facts to save automatically, drop, or seek consent for, while protecting sensitive information like passwords and personal data. Each saved memory links back to its originating chat and can be undone directly under the AI's reply. These adjustments aim to balance autonomous memory management with accuracy and privacy, addressing challenges in unsupervised AI memory systems and improving the assistants' usefulness for small-business workflows.

entry.title: Anthropic claims AI-assisted proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis in Lean; Stanford releases independent all-human competing draft hours later [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge announced a proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis using the AI model Claude, formalized in the Lean programming language with over 250,000 pages of verification. Shortly after, Stanford researchers published an independent, fully human-generated draft proof by mathematician Alessandro Masullo, which had undergone months of internal review. Both proofs are currently under scrutiny by the mathematical community to assess their validity and correctness. Alpöge's AI-assisted proof extends an approach involving chained mathematical transformations to mimic derivatives on number sequences, while Stanford's draft represents a traditional human effort. The Lean formalization acts as a digital referee to verify logical steps in the AI proof, though human experts must confirm the initial problem encoding. Stanford's draft was released earlier than planned due to Anthropic's announcement, and mathematicians are encouraged to review and translate it into formal verification systems to identify and resolve any gaps. The competing proofs highlight the evolving role of AI in mathematical research and the importance of rigorous peer review. Both approaches could potentially validate the long-standing hypothesis, which is central to number theory and has implications for many related mathematical theories.

entry.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a 26.4B-parameter looped transformer model that reprocesses layers per token to improve reasoning and runs on laptops [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Thinking Machines has introduced Inkling 2 Mini, an open-source looped transformer model with 26.4 billion parameters that runs certain layers multiple times per token to enhance internal reasoning without generating extra text. The model supports text and image processing, has a 1-million-token context window, and is licensed under Apache 2.0. It achieves performance comparable to Qwen3.8 27B on coding tests at roughly six times lower computational cost and four times the speed, according to Artificial Analysis. Inkling 2 Mini can run locally on Macs with at least 32 GB of memory and Nvidia's DGX Spark, with weights and a research version available on Hugging Face.

entry.title: US technology stocks post worst weekly drop since pandemic as Nasdaq 100 enters bear market amid AI skepticism and Nvidia SEC review [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: US technology stocks fell sharply last week, with the Nasdaq 100 dropping 10.4 percent and entering bear market territory, marking its worst weekly loss since the Covid-19 pandemic. The decline was driven by growing doubts about AI investments, a 14 percent plunge in Nvidia shares following an SEC accounting review, and a 9.1 percent drop in Anthropic's stock after its IPO. Additional factors contributing to the sell-off include concerns over chip and memory stock valuations amid their cyclical nature, political uncertainties after the recent midterm elections, and persistent inflation fueled by high oil prices due to the Iran war. The US semiconductor index also fell 10.7 percent, with losses across major companies such as Sandisk, Micron, and Broadcom.

entry.title: Marketing teams are expected to adopt GitHub within a year to manage AI-driven content and collaboration workflows [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Marketing teams increasingly rely on AI tools that require managing interconnected files and workflows, which traditional document platforms like Google Drive and SharePoint do not support effectively. GitHub offers version control, shared access, and vendor independence, making it suitable for marketing teams to store brand voice guides, positioning files, and AI skills in a centralized repository. Maya Pasek, Head of Content at Bluestone PIM, implemented GitHub for her marketing team to consolidate AI knowledge and automations, enabling seamless sharing and updates across team members regardless of the AI tool used. This approach helps maintain a consistent brand voice, facilitates collaboration, and allows easy switching between AI vendors without losing accumulated work.

entry.title: Dragos research finds three AI provider breaches and widespread prompt leaks, highlighting risks in AI supply chains and the need for canary token monitoring [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: Dragos conducted a five-month investigation by sending nearly two million unique AI prompts containing trackable canary tokens to various AI providers, uncovering three significant security breaches and unauthorized access to customer prompts. The study revealed that inference data often traverses multiple organizations and marketplaces, exposing sensitive information despite privacy settings. The research showed that some AI inference marketplaces and routers expose customer prompts through standard logging and fail to honor privacy policies, with data sometimes transmitted internationally without consent. Dragos emphasizes the importance of deploying canary tokens to detect prompt leaks and protect AI supply chains from ongoing vulnerabilities and data exposure.

entry.title: Pantry launches open source scanner for macOS, Linux, and Windows to check AI coding agents and repos for vulnerabilities and malware [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Pantry is an open source security tool that scans installed software and code repositories on macOS, Linux, and Windows machines to detect vulnerabilities and malware affecting AI coding agents. It identifies risky code that runs when repos are opened, including hidden scripts that can steal credentials, and flags unsafe third-party scripts without integrity checks. The tool cross-references installed package versions against vulnerability databases like OSV.dev and CISA KEV, reporting only relevant issues and suggesting safe updates. Pantry stores scan results locally for offline searching and can apply user-level fixes automatically, while requiring manual intervention for changes needing elevated permissions. It aims to secure machines before AI agents execute potentially harmful code from repositories or tools.

entry.title: Developer launches GURU, an Android app framework enabling personal AI agents to run commands and tools on-device with user-controlled permissions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: GURU is an Android app that provides a Linux shell environment and 390 tools, allowing language models to operate on the phone and network without root or accounts. Users supply their own AI model keys or run Ollama locally, and the app manages command execution with permission checks and error handling. It supports multiple AI agents with customizable instructions and tools, and includes privacy features like Tor routing and encrypted API key storage. The app fetches prompts, skills, and tools from a public server over Tor, enabling updates without app releases. It also plans a creator marketplace called Ottio for selling agents and other AI assets, alongside a future data marketplace and decentralized social network. The project is maintained by a single developer using AI-assisted coding and is currently in public beta with no external audits.

entry.title: Aletheia Aegis launches deterministic sub-millisecond output guard for AI agents to block credential leaks and life-safety failures with optional semantic review [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: Aletheia Aegis is a runtime safety platform designed to enforce deterministic, sub-millisecond checks on AI-generated outputs before they reach users. It blocks irreversible harms such as credential leaks and life-safety violations immediately, while optionally using a semantic judge for complex cases under strict controls. The system runs offline on CPU, retains no response text by default, and aims to provide fast, reliable safety for AI agents in regulated or high-throughput environments without the latency and cost of secondary model evaluations. The platform operates in two stages: a deterministic engine that performs pattern and structural checks at wire speed, and an optional semantic judge that reviews pre-redacted outputs for subjective issues. Aletheia Aegis is part of the broader Aletheia safety framework, which standardizes failure signatures across AI agent lifecycles and complements other tools that guard tool execution. Benchmarks show the system evaluates outputs in under 0.03 milliseconds on typical hardware, supporting scalable deployment in production settings.

entry.title: ClawDOS launches AI coding agent for DOS running on original IBM PC XT hardware with Turbo C integration [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: ClawDOS is an AI-powered coding assistant designed to run on the DOS operating system of an original IBM PC XT, using an 8088 processor at 4.77 MHz and 640K of RAM. It can read, edit, compile, and run programs using Turbo C, maintaining conversation state and interacting with the system through a DOS program called HARNESS.EXE. The project was created for experimentation and entertainment, demonstrating how AI can operate within the constraints of vintage hardware. ClawDOS relies on a separate "bridge" PC to handle TLS, which the 8088 cannot manage, while the main AI functions run natively on the DOS machine. It can generate code, compile it, execute it, and analyze output, showcasing an intersection of old and new technology.

entry.title: Meta re-evaluates 2030 net-zero emissions goal after reporting a 40% rise in carbon footprint due to AI data center expansion
entry.summary: Meta is reconsidering its 2030 net-zero emissions target following a record 40% increase in its carbon footprint from 2024 to 2025, driven largely by accelerated AI data center growth. The company's 2026 sustainability report highlights that demand for AI infrastructure has outpaced projections, prompting a reassessment of timelines and interim goals while maintaining transparency. Meta's total emissions rose from 15.6 million metric tonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2024 to over 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025, with net emissions increasing by 45% despite renewable energy investments and carbon removal efforts. The report also notes increased water consumption linked to power generation, underscoring challenges in balancing sustainability with rapid AI infrastructure expansion. Meta's public acknowledgment contrasts with other Big Tech firms that have so far maintained their original sustainability commitments.

entry.title: Researcher sends 2 million unique prompts through AI supply chain, finds widespread data leaks and compromised providers [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]

The experiment revealed significant leaks of sensitive information, including compromised hosting providers and resellers logging and misusing user data despite privacy flags. The study found that attackers accessed and reused stolen credentials to explore cloud resources and maintain persistent access. Some AI routers and inference marketplaces failed to honor end-user privacy settings, exposing data to unauthorized parties. These findings highlight serious security and privacy vulnerabilities in the current AI service ecosystem.

entry.title: OpenAI details layered defenses against adversarial distillation to protect model capabilities and reasoning traces in GPT-6.2 [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI has outlined its multi-faceted approach to combat adversarial distillation, a technique where unauthorized actors use outputs from advanced AI models to train new models without safeguards. The company focuses on protecting the internal reasoning steps, or chain-of-thought, that models generate, which can reveal sensitive capabilities if extracted. These protections are particularly critical in dual-use areas like cybersecurity and biology, where misuse could have harmful consequences. The updated safeguards in GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol significantly reduce the success rate of attacks attempting to extract protected reasoning, dropping from 54.0% to 0.2% in internal tests. OpenAI combines adversarial testing, model training improvements, classifiers, and API-level protections to detect and disrupt attempts to replicate its models' capabilities without authorization. This approach aims to prevent the transfer of advanced capabilities to less secure models that could be exploited for malicious purposes.

entry.title: Watch Duty uses Google's Gemini AI to transcribe wildfire radio dispatches in under 30 seconds, speeding up critical alerts [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Watch Duty, a nonprofit wildfire alert app staffed by firefighters and first responders, has deployed a Gemini-powered tool developed with Google.org Fellowship support to convert noisy fire radio transmissions into real-time text. This technology enables the detection of new wildfire dispatches in less than 30 seconds, improving alert speed and accuracy during emergencies. The tool reduces transcription errors on degraded VHF radio audio from 38% to 22.34% and processes over 200 hours of radio speech daily from about 400 active feeds, with capacity for over 10,000 feeds. It was instrumental during the July 2026 Railroad Fire in Washington, allowing Watch Duty to send its first nighttime Critical Alert and help residents evacuate before the fire reached homes. This development is part of a broader multi-year collaboration between Google and Watch Duty, including funding, cloud support, and integration with Google Search and Firebase Cloud Messaging to scale wildfire alerts nationwide. The partnership aims to provide faster, more reliable warnings to communities at risk of wildfires across all 50 states.

entry.title: OpenAI reduces success rate of extracting internal reasoning from GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol from 54% to 0.2% with new safeguards [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: OpenAI has significantly improved protections against extracting internal reasoning from its latest AI models, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol, reducing attack success rates in internal tests from 54% to 0.2%. The company also suspends thousands to tens of thousands of accounts weekly to combat coordinated distillation attacks. The new defenses include targeted training, input and output filters, and API restrictions that prevent older models from accessing protected reasoning. OpenAI is extending some of these improvements to GPT-6 Astra. Industry peers like Anthropic are also banning large numbers of accounts to fight similar attacks and have called for coordinated industry and policy responses.

entry.title: Signal blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and Android to prevent AI agents from accessing private chats, citing privacy risks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Signal has implemented restrictions on screenshots in iOS 27 and supported Android versions to prevent AI assistants like Apple's Siri AI, Google's Gemini Intelligence, and Meta's Muse from reading private chat content. The company described this as an "existential threat" to user privacy but acknowledged that protections remain incomplete, particularly on macOS where screenshots cannot be reliably blocked. The move addresses concerns that OS-level AI agents can capture decrypted messages directly from the screen, undermining end-to-end encryption. Signal has previously blocked Microsoft's Recall on Windows and urges Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide system-level controls to block AI agents from accessing app content entirely. Meta stated that its AI agent Muse accessed Signal content only with explicit user permission through broad setup permissions on Android and macOS.

entry.title: Google adds 'Computer Use' to Gemini Mac app to run desktop apps and complete tasks in background with live preview [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Google has introduced a new feature called "Computer Use" in its Gemini Mac app that allows the AI to perform multistep tasks across local files, desktop applications, and websites in an isolated background window. Users can describe their goals, and Gemini will navigate menus, click, and type to complete tasks while providing a live chat preview, enabling users to continue working uninterrupted. The feature lets users select which apps Gemini can access, watch the process live, pause it at any time, and approve key actions before execution. Examples include batch-editing photos, filling out shipping forms from PDFs, and creating presentations. "Computer Use" is rolling out in English in the US starting today, with the Gemini Mac app available for download.

entry.title: Bloomberg analysis finds AI-exposed job postings in China declined 10 percentage points faster than others amid labor market slowdown [ * ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A Bloomberg News analysis of nearly 10 million job postings from July 2021 to June 2025 shows that roles highly exposed to AI in China fell about 10 percentage points more than less affected jobs, indicating AI is intensifying challenges in the country's already weak labor market. Entry-level workers and the creative industry, including micro-drama production now largely AI-generated, are particularly impacted. Former central bank adviser Cai Fang warns a larger AI shock may be forthcoming. The analysis aligns with independent Chinese studies estimating significant net losses in new hires and wage declines linked to AI disruption, with roughly 70 million Chinese workers at risk compared to 45 million in the US. Chinese tech firms reportedly avoid citing AI as a layoff cause due to government and public backlash, though employees report substantial cuts. Job roles are also merging as AI enables single workers to perform tasks previously done by multiple people. The shift is evident in micro-dramas, where AI-generated content now accounts for over 90% of productions, reducing costs and production time but affecting incomes for actors and crews. China's youth unemployment remains high amid a crowded job market, prompting retraining efforts and government surveys on AI's labor impact. Similar employment declines among young workers in AI-exposed roles have been observed in the US and Australia, though economic factors complicate causal conclusions.
